query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a modest amount of titanium to the CoCrFeNi matrix will enable the in‐situ formation of a stable, lubricious titanium oxide phase on the sliding surface, thereby reducing both friction and wear across 25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that shows acceptable performance at room temperature but suffers from increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating a small (e.g., ~5–10 at.%) Ti addition to produce a variant such as AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5-like composition.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air from room temperature (≈25 °C) up to 800 °C under a moderate load (e.g., ≈1 N) that mimics the intended service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of dispersed nanometric Ti-based precipitates and a continuous, coherent oxide layer (likely TiO2 or mixed oxides) on the surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures the alloy retains its microstructural integrity while at elevated temperatures, the Ti addition oxidizes to form a protective and lubricious oxide film. This film minimizes direct metal–metal contact, reduces shear stresses, and thus decreases both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ti-modified alloy is expected to show a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate at both room temperature and at high temperatures (up to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy which exhibits acceptable low-friction/wear performance at room temperature but degrades when exposed to higher temperatures.
generation.boundary: Tested under sliding conditions in ambient (oxidative) atmosphere over a temperature range of 25 °C to 800 °C and under loads typical for tribological evaluation (e.g., ~1 N), where the kinetics of oxide formation are active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Ti content, the processing route to achieve the desired dispersion and oxide scale, and the magnitude of performance improvement remain to be calibrated. Moreover, the stability of the oxide film and potential phase changes in the modified alloy over prolonged exposure still require detailed evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the baseline equiatomic CoCrFeNi and another with an added ~5–10 at.% Ti (processed under identical conditions). Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in ambient air across the temperature range 25 °C to 800 °C under a controlled load (e.g., 1 N). After the tests, analyze the wear tracks and friction behavior using SEM, EDS, and XRD to assess the presence, continuity, and composition of any oxide layers.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss and volume loss) at each temperature
Surface oxide layer thickness and phase composition (via SEM/EDS/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the baseline across the test temperature range or if a coherent, lubricious oxide film does not form on its sliding surface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
